extracted.intended_audience: seamen, navigators, and scientific observers (astronomers, meteorologists, natural philosophers; members of the Royal Society)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical, empirical observation protocols and interpretive guidance for seafaring observers, astronomers, and natural philosophers (e.g., how to record compass variation, tides, celestial events, barometer readings, and biological/earth observations). Includes recommended instruments, measurement technique, and what particulars to record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observe the declination (variation) of the compass
rubrics_metrics.description: To observe the declination of the compass, or its variation from the meridian; noting also the latitude and longitude of the place where such observation is made, and stating the method of taking them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record compass variation together with the precise latitude and longitude of the observation and explicitly state the method used to determine those coordinates (so any later user can interpret/compare observations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Carry dipping needles and observe inclination
rubrics_metrics.description: To carry dipping needles with them, and observe their inclination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bring dipping needles as instruments to measure magnetic inclination (dip) and record the observed angle/inclination at each locality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observe tides carefully (times, heights, currents)
rubrics_metrics.description: To observe carefully the tides in as many places as they can, with all the circumstances; such as the precise time of ebbing and flowing in rivers, and at capes; the set of their currents, the perpendicular distance between the highest tide and lowest ebb, in spring and neap tides; what day of the moon's age, and what times of the year, the highest and lowest tides happen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For each tidal observation record precise times of ebb and flow, current direction ('set'), vertical range between highest and lowest tides for spring and neap, the lunar age/day and time of year when extremes occur. Correlate tidal behaviour with lunar phase and seasonal timing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make plots and draughts of coasts and ports
rubrics_metrics.description: To make plots and draughts of coasts, promontories, islands and ports, marking the bearings and distances as near as may be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Produce coastal charts with bearings and estimated distances; aim for best possible accuracy when marking promontories, islands and port approaches so charts can be compared and improved by later observers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sound and mark depths near shore
rubrics_metrics.description: To sound and mark the depths of coasts, ports, and other places near the shore.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take systematic depth soundings and annotate charts/plots with depth measurements to aid navigation. Combine with notes on the nature of the sea-bottom (see related criterion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Record nature of bottom in soundings
rubrics_metrics.description: To observe, in all soundings, the nature of the ground at the bottom of the sea, whether it be clay, sand, rock, &c.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When taking a sounding, describe the seabed composition (clay, sand, rock, etc.) so that depth data are accompanied by substrate type for anchoring/navigation and scientific use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep a register of all changes of wind and weather
rubrics_metrics.description: To keep a register of all changes of the wind and weather at all hours, both day and night, the point the wind blows from, and whether strong or weak; the rains, hail, snow, &c., the precise times of their beginnings and continuance, especially hurricanes and spouts; and above all, carefully to observe the trade-winds, about what degrees of latitude and longitude they first begin, where and when they cease, or change, or grow stronger or weaker, and how much.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain continuous logs of wind direction and strength, precipitation types and precise start/end times, and track trade-wind behaviour with approximate lat/long of onset, cessation and intensity changes. These registers should support later synthesis of climatological and navigational patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observe extraordinary meteors and celestial phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: To observe all extraordinary meteors, lightnings, thunders, ignes fatui, comets, &c., marking the places and times of their appearing, continuance, &c.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record occurrences of unusual atmospheric or celestial events with time and location, and note duration and other particulars to allow correlation between observers and regions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collect sea-water samples to measure weight/salinity
rubrics_metrics.description: To carry with them good scales, and glass-vials of about a pint, with narrow mouths, to be filled with sea-water in different latitudes, in order to know its weight, both of the water near the surface and at greater depths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bring scales and narrow-mouthed vials to sample surface and deeper sea-water at various latitudes; weigh samples to estimate specific weight (salinity) differences by latitude and depth. Preserve careful provenance (lat/long and depth) for each sample.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method to find the true distance of Sun and Moon by observed parallax
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed method: at certain times agreed on by two observers, using large and proper telescopes, with a measuring rod placed within the eye-glass at a convenient distance to serve for measuring small distances to minutes and seconds; let each observe the visible way of the moon among the fixed stars by taking her exact distance from any fixed star in or near her way, with the exact time and apparent diameter of her disk; continuing observations for two or three hours so two exact observations of her apparent place being made at two places distant in latitude and nearly under the same meridian, hence her true and exact distance may be collected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use synchronized observations by two observers at different latitudes nearly under the same meridian, large telescopes, and an in-eyepiece measuring rod to measure small angular separations to arcminutes/seconds. Record exact times, moon–star separations, and the moon's apparent diameter; repeat observations over two–three hours. Also: observe total lunar eclipses and solar eclipses—measure greatest obscuration relative to apparent solar diameter—to support distance derivation. Best observing times: about a quarter moon (four or five days before/after change), when the moon passes near/over fixed stars, or during total lunar eclipses; these allow close passage by telescopic stars and improved parallax determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observe Saturn with long telescopes and report ring structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Observation (example): with a very good telescope near 38 feet long and a double eye-glass, Saturn appeared distinct and suggested that Saturn is surrounded not by one circular body or ring only, but by two. Further observation of this appearance is earnestly recommended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use long focal-length telescopes and appropriate eyepieces to resolve planetary ring structure; report detailed descriptions and encourage repeated observations to confirm ring morphology (e.g., single vs multiple rings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Barometer: instrument purpose, apparatus choice, and empirical interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: The barometer is an instrument for measuring the weight of the atmosphere, founded on Torricelli's experiment; it is a glass tube filled with mercury, sealed at one end and immersed in stagnant mercury. Practical note: some wheel-barometers are hard to fill without air; the mercurial cylinder of narrow bore and thick glass is preferred for note-taking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance:
A. Instrument/handling: prefer narrow-bore mercurial cylinders of thick glass for stable readings; be aware wheel-barometers may trap air and be less reliable. Use multiple tubes/vessels to confirm indications. Place a wind-vane and consider an index of wind near the tube for concurrent wind direction records. Note approximate elevation relative to sea level when reporting readings.

B. Empirical correlations & interpretive rules (observed patterns summarized from many notes):
- Mercury seldom rose much above ~30 inches in the observers' records; rare excursions outside ~28–30 inches.
- Mercury often ascends higher in cold mornings and evenings than at warmer mid-day; rises in clear, settled/fair weather and in sun-shiny conditions, possibly due to vapour weight and heat effects.
- Mercury generally falls in rainy weather (air lighter with vapours), in windy weather (lateral motion reducing downward pressure), and often descends after rain.
- Mercury tends to be higher with east/north winds and lower with south/west winds (empirical association).
- Large changes in the air (e.g., dewy nights or remote rain) sometimes occur without noticeable barometer response; conversely, barometer sometimes falls with little immediate visible cause.
- Rapid rises in mercury after rain often indicate approaching settled serenity; falling mercury after rain may indicate ensuing broken/showery weather.
- Very large instantaneous changes are uncommon (greatest observed change ~2–2.5 inches); typical significant falls accompany storms and variable weather.
- Keep systematic notes across dates/times to correlate mercury with wind direction, precipitation, cloudiness and temperature; an external wind-vane and indexed wind chart improves interpretability.

C. Recording practice: record precise dates/times, local wind-vane readings, any nearby precipitation or cloud events, and instrument configuration for reproducible comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additional barometer interpretive note (Dr. Wallis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dr. Wallis never observed quicksilver higher than 30 inches nor lower than 28 inches (within ~1/4 inch). He observed quicksilver rise in thick foggy weather (ascribing this to heavy vapours) and in sun-shiny weather; in rainy weather it falls; in windy weather it generally falls more discernibly than in rain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Dr. Wallis' summary as additional empirical rule-of-thumb: expect barometer typically 28–30 inches in temperate inland sites; interpret rises in fog/sunny conditions as due to vapour/heating effects and falls in rain/high wind as typical. Note that local geography (e.g., elevation relative to sea level) should be reported.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimentally determine viper venom source and effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Redi's assertions: (1) The poison of vipers is neither in their teeth, nor in their tail, nor in their gall; but in two vesicles or bladders which cover their teeth, which when compressed emit a yellowish liquor that runs along the teeth and poisons the wound. (2) He asserts that ingestion of parts thought most poisonous in a viper did not produce considerable ill effects in his experiments. (3) He disputes various ancient/modern claims (e.g., that spittle of a fasting person kills vipers), ridiculing many ascribed antipathies and properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test venom location by observing secretion from vesicles upon compression and by rubbing wounds with gall vs venous liquid to compare effects (as Redi did). Note that later commentators/correctors observed that venom delivery occurs through perforated fangs (internal canals) and that some residue in fangs can still poison via pricking; later experiments (Fontana) showed fatality upon forced ingestion in some small animals, so ingestion safety claims must be treated cautiously. Report experimental protocols, doses, routes (wound rubbing vs ingestion), and species tested; include negative and contradictory evidence in the report.

rubrics_metrics.name: Earthquake observation: record multi-site reports and successive propagation
rubrics_metrics.description: Account of a small earthquake felt at divers places near Oxford; it was not noticed simultaneously at all places but moved successively from one locality to another. Observers should compare experiences at multiple villages/towns; ask about local intensity (e.g., movement of stones in rooms), and relate to local geology (e.g., hills stored with mineral substances).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When documenting seismic events, collect time-stamped reports from multiple localities, note sequence and local intensity, and seek any geological context (mineral deposits or hills) that might bear on local amplification. Do not assume simultaneity—record reported progression across sites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observe Jupiter spots to determine planetary rotation
rubrics_metrics.description: Observe permanent spots in the disk of Jupiter (two sorts: shadows of satellites and spots resembling lunar/solar spots); track their motion from east to west and note that apparent motion is unequal (swifter near the centre than the circumference). One observed spot's periodic revolution was estimated at 9 hours 56 minutes (by repeated observations and ephemerides).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeatedly observe identifiable spots on Jupiter, note their disk position and time, and compute apparent period by tracking recurrence to the same central position; document observational conditions (telescope focal length/eyepiece), and include ephemerides for multi-year comparison. Note that spots may disappear and reappear; document such discontinuities and possible solar-spot-like nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report and compare disputing astronomical observations
rubrics_metrics.description: When a dispute arises between observers (e.g., M. Hevelius and M. Auzout concerning a comet's observed position), compare printed writings, consult telescope observations at home, and compare relative positions of the comet to telescopic stars; weigh the truth of each relation but determine course by aggregate observations across observers/locations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resolve conflicting astronomical reports by: (1) collating printed descriptions, (2) consulting independent local telescopic observations and comparing the comet's relative position to nearby telescopic stars, (3) soliciting and incorporating confirmations from observers in multiple countries. Use consensus of independent records to adjudicate discrepancies and publish the reconciled result.
